raw_case_text:
The investigations arose from the proband, a 48-year-old female of Asian origin who was previously well other than a history of schizophrenia, presenting to the hospital with 6 months of persistent cough and worsening breathlessness. Chest imaging revealed diffuse ground glass opacities. The patient rapidly deteriorated and required intubation for severe type I respiratory failure requiring veno-venous extra-corporeal membrane oxygenation assistance. The clinical course of the patient is as described in  Supplementary Figure S1A . Bronchoalveolar lavage examination revealed Pneumocystis jirovecii on microscopy. Treatment with trimethoprim-cotrimoxazole (TMP-SMX) and adjunctive corticosteroids was promptly initiated. Despite repeat negative HIV tests, the patient had an absolute CD4+ count of 25 cells/microl. Over 6 weeks, she progressively improved before discharge 3 months later. As her CD4+ counts had remained consistently low, the patient was prescribed long-term TMP-SMX as a secondary prophylaxis and remained stable.
Given that the atypicality of the clinical course was suggestive of underlying immunodeficiency, whole exome sequencing was performed. The sequencing revealed two heterozygous rare variants of TRAP1 on chromosome 16p13 (GRCh37): one at g.3739109 C>G (exon 3) resulting in amino acid switch from Glutamate-to-Glutamine at protein position 93 (E93Q) ( Figure 1A ) and another at g.3740885 C>T (exon 2) resulting in alanine-to-threonine switch at position 64 (A64T) ( Figure 1A ). Both E93Q and A64T SNPs lie in the N-terminal ATP-binding domain (NTD) of TRAP1 and were predicted to be deleterious in-silico ( Figure 1B ;  Supplementary Table S1 ).
Western blot and qRT-PCR analysis of the patient's peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) revealed diminished TRAP1 expression and transcript ( Figure 1C ,  Supplementary Figure S1B ). TRAP1 had previously been shown to protect against apoptosis. In line with those data, we observed increased cleaved, active caspase-3 and caspase-7 in the patient's cells, which may be associated with an overall decline in TRAP1 expression ( Figure 1C ). Caspase-3 mediates apoptosis by activating Cyclophilin D (CypD), an isomerase that regulates the mitochondrial permeability transition pore. This pore allows the release of pro-apoptotic factors from the mitochondria into the cytoplasm, initiating mitochondria-mediated apoptosis. Indeed, CypD was accentuated ( Figure 1C ), in line with caspase-3 augmentation in the patient's cells.
As caspase 3 can co-activate caspase-1, the downstream mediator of inflammasome activation that leads to interleukin-1 beta (IL-1beta) secretion, we stained for cleaved caspase 1 and IL-1beta. We observed increased caspase-1 cleavage and mature IL-1beta in the patient's cells treated with TLR1/2 or TLR4 ligands, suggesting that the mutant TRAP1s exacerbate inflammasome activation ( Figures 1C, E ,  Supplementary Figure S1C ). However, the aggravated apoptosis exerted a limited inhibitory effect on the NFkappaB complex through NFkappaB2, NFkappaB1, and RelB ( Figure 1D ).
When plasmids containing WT or mutant TRAP1 (E93Q, A64T, or the double E93Q/A64T mutant) were transfected into A549 cells, any mutant, whether single or double, was expressed lower compared to the WT protein itself. The mutants re-capitulated the immunotypic phenotype as was observed in the patient: enhanced cleaved caspase-3, caspase-7, and CypD. Of note, enhanced caspase activity was more evident in E93Q over A64T in line with in-silico prediction, and an additive effect was observed with co-expressed E93Q-A64T double mutant ( Figure 1E ). As was observed in patient cells, mutant TRAP1 reduced NFkappaB signaling, with the most prominent inhibitory effect on NFkappaB1, RelB and p65 activity observed in double E93Q/A64T mutant.
As the presentation with PjP suggested that the effects of mutant TRAP1 was exacerbated during PjP infection, we infected TRAP1-transfected A549 human lung cells with P. jiroveci. Compared against WT-TRAP1, cells expressing the A64T or E93Q variant displayed reduced viability to P. jiroveci infection. In particular, dual E93Q/A64T-transfected cells exhibited highest cell loss (>80%) ( Figure 1F ).
The increased apoptotic markers found in patient PBMCs in the presence of idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia suggest that CD4+ T cells are especially sensitive to TRAP1 dysfunction. To confirm this hypothesis, patient cells were treated with staurosporine to induce apoptosis. At rest and 6 hours after staurosporine treatment, the patient's PBMC gated on CD4+ cells showed elevated annexin-V-positive, propodium iodide(PI)-negative cells in the apoptotic stage compared to healthy controls. Following staurosporine, the patient's annexin-V-positive, PI-positive cells marking cell death significantly doubled ( Figure 1G ). Collectively, our results suggest that the patient's CD4+ lymphopenia was a result of increased apoptosis.
As TRAP1 regulates mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and suppresses ROS production, we next evaluated the effect of TRAP1 mutation on ROS production. Total ROS production, as measured by 2',7'-dichlorofluorescein, was incrementally elevated in mutant-TRAP1 cells relative to WT ( Figure 2A ; top panel). Specifically, when stained with mito-SOX which probed specifically for mito-ROS, the frequency and median fluorescence intensity of E93Q- and A64T-transfected cells increased relative to WT ( Figure 2A ; bottom panel). Notably, dual-E93Q/A64T cells had 6-fold increased mito-ROS ( Figure 2A ; bottom panel). Similarly, the patient's PBMC demonstrated markedly increased total and mito-ROS ( Figure 2B ).
As previous studies have shown the involvement of TRAP1 in regulating OXPHOS and glycolysis, Seahorse Mito Stress and glycolytic rate assays were performed on A549 cells transfected with the respective TRAP1 variants. Compared to cells transfected with WT-TRAP1 or empty vector, the double E93Q/A64T mutant expressing cells had the most markedly reduced mitochondrial respiration over the single mutants, as measured by the Mito-Stress assay ( Figure 2C ). To determine if the OXPHOS defects were due to electron transport chain (ETC) defects, we ran a BN-PAGE to look at the ETC complexes. There were no differences, suggesting that TRAP1 altered the efficiencies of ETC complexes rather than their assembly ( Supplementary Figure S2 ). Similar to the observed decrease in mitochondrial respiration, the double mutant displayed a guarded reduction in the ability to increase glycolysis when the electron transport chain was blocked ( Figure 2D ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old Asian female presented with a 6-month history of persistent cough and progressively worsening breathlessness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had been previously physically well, experienced 6 months of persistent cough and progressive dyspnea prior to hospital presentation, where she rapidly deteriorated into severe type I respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of schizophrenia; otherwise previously healthy with no known history of immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic cough and progressive breathlessness for 6 months.

objective.physical_examination: Rapid respiratory deterioration into severe type I respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO).
objective.advanced_workup: Chest imaging: Diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) microscopy: Directly identified Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms. Lymphocyte subsets: Profound idiopathic CD4+ T-cell lymphocytopenia with an absolute CD4+ count of 25 cells/μL. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) and functional immunogenetics: Identified compound/double rare heterozygous missense variants in the N-terminal ATP-binding domain of TRAP1 on chromosome 16p13 (GRCh37): g.3739109C>G (exon 3, p.Glu93Gln / E93Q) and g.3740885C>T (exon 2, p.Ala64Thr / A64T). PBMC and A549 functional assays demonstrated diminished TRAP1 protein/mRNA expression, increased cleaved caspase-3, caspase-7, and Cyclophilin D (CypD), heightened caspase-1/IL-1beta inflammasome activation, reduced NF-kappaB signaling, 6-fold increased mitochondrial ROS (mito-SOX), impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and glycolytic reserve on Seahorse assays, and accelerated CD4+ T-cell apoptosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Life-threatening Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by BAL microscopy) requiring VV-ECMO, secondary to idiopathic CD4+ T-cell lymphocytopenia (CD4+ count 25 cells/μL) driven by deleterious digenic/compound heterozygous TRAP1 variants (p.E93Q and p.A64T) causing mitochondrial dysfunction, excess mitochondrial ROS, and accelerated CD4+ T-cell apoptosis. Plan and clinical course: Managed with endotracheal intubation, VV-ECMO support, intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), and adjunctive corticosteroids. She progressively improved over 6 weeks, was discharged after 3 months, and remained clinically stable on long-term secondary TMP-SMX prophylaxis due to persistently low CD4+ counts.
